hints.A: Mechanism (verified diagnosis): For malformed input such as "<base <base <base ..." with no '>' anywhere, the regex engine attempts a match at every occurrence of "<base" followed by whitespace. At each such start, the attribute-span part of the pattern ([^>]*) consumes all remaining text up to the end of the string, because no '>' exists, and then backtracks character by character looking for "href". Every one of the n start positions therefore scans O(n) characters, giving O(n^2) total work. The cost comes from the attribute-span part of the pattern, not from the URL capture group and not from the surrounding Python function.
hints.B: Repair principle (design level): Bound the work of each failed match attempt so that its scan cannot extend beyond the tag in which it started. The attribute scan of one tag should stop at a character that cannot legitimately appear in that tag's attribute area, so that in malformed input it stops at the next tag start instead of the end of the document. Do NOT use a fixed numeric length limit: valid base tags may contain other attributes of any length before href, and those must still match. Prefer a minimal change to the existing pattern over rewriting the function or adding a new code path.
hints.C:
Analogous example from a different codebase (not this file): a pattern
    _item_re = re.compile(r"\[item\s[^\]]*key=(\w+)")
was quadratic on input "[item " * n with no closing ']', because [^\]]* ran to the end of the text from every "[item" start. It was repaired by also excluding the opening delimiter from the span class, so each attempt stops at the next "[":
    _item_re = re.compile(r"\[item\s[^\[\]]*key=(\w+)")
Normal inputs such as "[item a=1 long_attr=xxxx key=abc]" still match. Apply the corresponding idea to this file's pattern yourself.
hints.G:
Regex performance repair checklist (generic; written for any super-linear regex issue, not for this file):
1. Identify the unbounded span (X*, [^c]*, .*) that can run far past the point where a match could still succeed, and the inputs on which the overall match fails.
2. Lazy quantifiers (*?, +?) change which match is preferred, but when the match FAILS the engine still explores the same positions; they usually do not remove super-linear behaviour.
3. Fixed numeric bounds such as {0,100} hide the symptom but reject legitimate long inputs; avoid them unless the specification mandates a limit.
4. Effective repairs make failed attempts cheap and non-overlapping: restrict the span's character class so it cannot cross a token that would begin a new candidate match, or split/tokenize the input first so each region is scanned once.
5. Keep the change minimal and make sure every previously valid input, including ones with extra or long content inside the span, still matches.
